title: Hear, O Israel: Love the LORD with Everything
summary: Moses gives the heart of the whole law: the LORD is one, and Israel must love him with all their heart, soul, and strength. These words are to be taught to children, spoken of through every part of the day, and marked on hands, foreheads, doorposts, and gates. He warns that prosperity in the new land will tempt Israel to forget the God who freed them, and he tells parents how to answer when a child asks what the commandments mean.
story:
In chapter 5 Moses repeated the Ten Commandments and recalled how the people, terrified by God's voice at Horeb (another name for Sinai), begged him to hear the rest of God's words for them. Chapter 6 begins to deliver those words, and it starts not with a rule about sacrifice or property but with love. Chapters 5 to 11 form a long appeal to loyalty before the detailed laws of chapters 12 to 26, and within that appeal chapters 6 to 11 read like an extended sermon on the first commandment, no other gods. This chapter sets the tone for everything after it.

The people are about to move from a wilderness where they depended on God for daily bread into a land of cities, cisterns, and vineyards they did not build. Moses knows that abundance can do what hunger could not: make them forget. So the chapter moves from a confession (who God is) to a command (love him with everything) to a strategy (keep his words in every room and hour of life) to a warning (plenty breeds forgetfulness) and finally to a script for the next generation, whose questions are to be answered with a story of rescue. The same pattern runs through the rest of Deuteronomy, and the chapter's first paragraph became the confession Jews have recited morning and evening for well over two thousand years.
historical:
The setting is the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, in the fortieth year after the exodus (1:1-5), where Moses addresses the generation about to cross into Canaan. When the book reached its present form is debated. Tradition, Jewish and Christian, attributes it to Moses. Since W. M. L. de Wette's dissertation of 1805, most critical scholars have connected at least its core with the law book found in the temple in the eighteenth year of King Josiah, about 622 BC (2 Kings 22-23), and see its final shape as the work of the late monarchy and the exile. Others, among them Kenneth Kitchen (On the Reliability of the Old Testament, 2003), argue that its covenant form best matches Hittite treaties of the second millennium BC and so supports an early origin. The book introduction sets out the positions; what matters here is that every view reads the chapter against ancient treaty language.

That language is most visible in the command to love. In 1963 William L. Moran (Catholic Biblical Quarterly 25) showed that in ancient Near Eastern diplomacy to love a king meant to be loyal to him and serve him alone. The clearest example is the Succession Treaty that the Assyrian king Esarhaddon imposed in 672 BC to secure the throne for his son Ashurbanipal. Copies were excavated at Nimrud (ancient Kalhu) under Max Mallowan in 1955, and another was found in 2009 in a temple at Tell Tayinat in southern Turkey, showing that such oaths were displayed in subject kingdoms of the west, not far from Israel and Judah. The treaty requires the subject peoples to love Ashurbanipal as themselves, to guard the oath for their children and descendants, and to reject any rival. Deuteronomy 6 uses the same vocabulary for Israel's bond with God, but it roots Israel's love in God's prior love for their fathers (4:37; 7:7-8; 10:15), which no Assyrian king claimed. The only other place in the Hebrew Bible where the triad of heart, soul, and strength (me'od) recurs is the verdict on Josiah, the king who turned to the LORD with all three (2 Kings 23:25).

The confession that the LORD is one also had a concrete setting. Inscriptions on storage jars from Kuntillet Ajrud, a way station in the northern Sinai from about 800 BC, invoke blessing by YHWH of Samaria and YHWH of Teman, and pair him with Asherah. They show that some Israelites spoke of the one God in local forms and gave him a consort. The inscriptions have led some scholars to ask whether the Shema's insistence that YHWH is one also answered that habit; whatever its exact force, it excludes any such division of Israel's loyalty.

The chapter's later life is well documented. The Letter of Aristeas (2nd century BC, sections 158-159) mentions God's words set on gates and doors and a sign worn on the hands. Josephus (Antiquities 4.213) describes the same practices in the first century AD. Tefillin (phylacteries, small leather cases holding handwritten passages) and mezuzot were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran; Yigael Yadin published a set in 1969, and several include passages later rabbinic practice did not, such as the Ten Commandments. The Nash Papyrus, a single Hebrew sheet bought in Egypt in 1898 by W. L. Nash and now in Cambridge University Library, contains the Ten Commandments followed by the Shema. Stanley Cook published it in 1903, and William F. Albright's study of 1937 dated it to the second or first century BC. The Mishnah (compiled about AD 200) says the priests in the temple recited the Ten Commandments and the three paragraphs of the Shema each morning (m. Tamid 5:1), and the Babylonian Talmud (Berakhot 12a) explains that the Ten Commandments were later dropped from daily prayer outside the temple because of heretics who claimed that only they had been given at Sinai.
cultural:
The word Shema, Hebrew for hear, gives this confession its name. In Hebrew, to hear is also to heed; the same verb covers listening and obeying. The body language of the chapter would have made sense to a first reader. The heart (levav) in Hebrew thought is not mainly the seat of feeling but of thinking, choosing, and purpose. The soul (nefesh) is the whole living self, one's very life. The third term, usually translated strength, is the ordinary Hebrew word for very or much, used here as a noun: love God with all your muchness, everything you have. The Aramaic translation known as Targum Onkelos renders it with a word for wealth, and the Mishnah (m. Berakhot 9:5) reads the three as the good and evil impulses together, one's life even to martyrdom, and one's money. Together they mean the whole person and everything in the person's hand.

Ancient readers would also have heard the command to love as the language of covenant loyalty, and so it is not strange to them that love is commanded. Deuteronomy nonetheless fills the word with warmth: it speaks of God setting his affection on Israel's fathers (10:15) and promises that God himself will one day circumcise Israel's heart so that they can love him (30:6). The command expects feeling, but it does not wait for it. Love here is a settled allegiance shown in listening, remembering, and obeying.

Verses 7 to 9 cover every place and time in an ancient household: sitting at home and walking on the road, lying down and getting up, the hand that works and the forehead between the eyes, the doorpost of the house and the gate of the town, where elders met and justice was done (Ruth 4:1). The doorpost had already marked Israelite houses on the night of the Passover (Exodus 12:7). Jewish tradition came to observe verses 8 and 9 literally with tefillin and the mezuzah, a small case holding verses 4 to 9 and 11:13 to 21 fixed to the doorframe. Karaite Jews and many Christian interpreters have read the verses as a vivid figure for keeping God's words constantly before one's mind and deeds, much as Proverbs tells the student to bind wisdom on the neck and write it on the tablet of the heart (Proverbs 3:3; 7:3). Jesus assumes the practice when he criticizes those who make their phylacteries broad for show (Matthew 23:5). Both readings agree that faith was meant to fill ordinary life, not stay in a sanctuary.

The land Israel is promised was a land of hill-country towns where survival depended on cisterns cut into rock to hold the winter rains, terraced vineyards, and olive groves that take years to bear. To receive cities, full houses, cisterns, vineyards, and olive trees all at once was to receive generations of other people's labor. The oath of verse 13 also had a social setting: in the ancient world one swore by the god one trusted to punish perjury, so to swear by the LORD alone was to name him alone as the judge of one's word (compare Jeremiah 12:16). The child's question of verse 20 fits a household where the laws were visibly kept at table, in the calendar, and at the door, and where children naturally asked why. Exodus 12:26-27, 13:14, and Joshua 4:6-7 build the same question into Israel's rites and memorials.
literary:
The chapter is a sermon built around a single confession, and it is framed by a word in the singular. Verse 1 opens with ‘this is the commandment’ (hammitsvah), followed by the plural statutes and ordinances, and verse 25 closes with ‘all this commandment’. Norbert Lohfink's study Das Hauptgebot (‘The Main Commandment’, 1963) argued that chapters 5 to 11 expound one great commandment, exclusive loyalty to the LORD, of which the later laws are applications.

Within the frame the movement is clear. Verses 1 to 3 introduce the teaching with a call to hear and obey, and the call to hear in verse 3 is repeated at once in verse 4. Verses 4 and 5 state the confession (six Hebrew words with no verb) and the command (a threefold ‘with all’). Verses 6 to 9 spread the command outward from the heart to the children, the house, the road, the body, and the town gate, using paired opposites (sitting and walking, lying down and rising) to mean all of life. Verses 10 to 19 turn to warning, with a hammering series of negatives: cities you did not build, houses you did not fill, cisterns you did not dig, vineyards and olive trees you did not plant. The warning is one long conditional sentence whose main clause arrives only in verse 12, so that the reader feels the weight of the gifts before hearing the danger. The chapter closes with a catechism, a child's question and the parent's answer (verses 20 to 25), which retells the exodus in the first person plural, ‘we were slaves’. In 1938 Gerhard von Rad called verses 20 to 24, with 26:5-9 and Joshua 24:2-13, a ‘short historical creed’; his larger theory about these creeds is now widely doubted, but his observation that Israel confessed its faith by telling what God had done has lasted.

The chapter also belongs to a larger pattern. Deuteronomy 11:18-21 repeats verses 6 to 9 almost word for word, framing the sermon of chapters 6 to 11. Jewish liturgy joined 6:4-9 with 11:13-21 and Numbers 15:37-41 as the three paragraphs of the Shema. Like much of Deuteronomy, the chapter shifts between singular and plural ‘you’, addressing Israel now as one person and now as a crowd; older critics used the shifts to separate sources, while many recent readers hear them as rhetoric that stresses Israel's unity before God.

outline.t: Keep the commands so that you may live and prosper
The Shema: the LORD is one; love him with all you are
Do not forget the LORD in the land of plenty
When your son asks: the story behind the commands

doctrines.note: The Shema confesses that Israel's God is one: not one god among many, but the only LORD, owed undivided loyalty. The Christian doctrine of the Trinity does not set this aside; the church has always confessed one God, and the New Testament writers, all of them formed by the Shema, confessed Jesus as Lord within it (1 Corinthians 8:6).

The first thing asked of Israel is love, and love of the whole person: heart, life, and every resource. Because it is commanded, it is first a matter of allegiance and will, and because Deuteronomy grounds it in God's prior love (7:7-8) and promises that God will make it possible (30:6), it is response rather than achievement. Jesus names it the greatest commandment.

The chapter pairs love with fear (verses 2, 13, and 24). Fear of the LORD here is reverent loyalty, the stance of a people who know whom they serve, and it is the aim of the teaching across three generations. Love and fear are not rivals in Deuteronomy but two sides of one relationship.

Faith is to be passed on in the home, through daily conversation and honest answers to children's questions. The chapter gives parents a script that begins with the story of rescue before it gets to rules, and it treats a child's question as welcome, not as a threat.

The danger Moses fears is not hardship but comfort. When Israel eats and is satisfied, they may forget the God who brought them out of slavery and follow the gods of the peoples around them. Forgetting comes before following, and prosperity is named as a spiritual threat.

words.note: Shama, to hear. One of the most common verbs in the Hebrew Bible, it occurs more than 1,100 times. The standard lexicons (BDB, HALOT) trace its range from perceiving a sound to listening attentively to obeying, and in covenant contexts it often means all three at once. The call “Hear, O Israel” (verses 3 and 4) is therefore a summons to attention and obedience together, and Deuteronomy's chain of verbs (hear, keep, do) begins here. The imperative gives the Shema its name.

Echad, one, the ordinary Hebrew numeral, used about 970 times. In verse 4 it can mean ‘one’ (a statement of God's unity or uniqueness) or ‘alone’ (Israel's God is the LORD and no other), and translations divide accordingly. Christian writers have sometimes argued that echad implies a compound unity because it is used of the ‘one flesh’ of marriage (Genesis 2:24), but that reads a single context into a common word. The weight of the verse falls on the LORD being the only God and wholly Israel's.

Ahav, to love. The verb, used over two hundred times, covers family love, friendship, desire, and in treaty contexts loyal allegiance. Deuteronomy uses it in both directions: God loved Israel's fathers and chose their offspring (4:37; 7:8), and Israel is to love God (6:5; 10:12; 11:1; 30:6). That it is commanded shows that biblical love is first a settled commitment of the will, though Deuteronomy's warm language shows it is never less than affection.

Me'od, very, much, exceedingly. It occurs about 300 times, almost always as an adverb (Genesis 1:31, ‘very good’). Only here and in 2 Kings 23:25, which echoes this verse of King Josiah, is it used as a noun for the whole of one's capacity, hence ‘strength’ or ‘might’. Targum Onkelos and the Mishnah (m. Berakhot 9:5) took it to include wealth, a reading that fits the chapter's concern with the goods of the land.

Shanan, to sharpen. The verb is rare, used fewer than ten times, mostly of swords, arrows, and sharp tongues (Deuteronomy 32:41; Psalm 45:5; 64:3). Verse 7 is its only use for teaching, rendered ‘teach diligently’ or ‘impress’. Rashi, following the early midrash Sifre, took it to mean the words should be sharp and ready in your mouth; others connect it with shanah, ‘to repeat’. Either way, the teaching pictured is deliberate and repeated, not occasional.

Yare, to fear, revere. The verb occurs more than 300 times and ranges from terror (Genesis 3:10) to reverent awe and loyal worship. Deuteronomy uses it for the right stance before God (4:10; 10:12, 20), and in this chapter it frames the whole: the teaching aims at fear across generations (verse 2), fear stands first among the commands against idolatry (verse 13), and fear is named again in the parent's answer (verse 24). Here it is not dread but reverence that keeps the covenant.

Shakach, to forget. It occurs about a hundred times, and Deuteronomy uses it repeatedly as the great danger of life in the land (4:9, 23; 8:11-19; 9:7). In Hebrew, forgetting is less a lapse of memory than a failure of loyalty, as remembering means acting on what one knows. Verse 12 makes it the first step toward other gods: Israel will not decide to abandon the LORD so much as stop remembering him while enjoying his gifts.

Tsedaqah, righteousness. It occurs about 157 times and names right conduct within a relationship: faithfulness to what a covenant requires, and in God's case his saving faithfulness. Deuteronomy 24:13 uses the same phrase as verse 25, where returning a poor man's cloak ‘will be righteousness for you before the LORD’. The word here describes covenant faithfulness that God recognizes, not a payment that earns a place in the covenant; how it relates to Paul's use is discussed under the hard questions.

christ:
When a scribe asked Jesus which commandment is the most important, he answered with this chapter: “Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One” and the command to love God with all one's heart, soul, mind, and strength, joined to the command to love one's neighbor from Leviticus 19:18 (Mark 12:29-31). Only Mark includes the confession itself; Matthew 22:37-40 adds that all the Law and the Prophets hang on the two commands, and in Luke 10:25-28 a lawyer gives the same pairing and Jesus answers with the parable of the Good Samaritan. Jesus did not replace the Shema with a new creed. He placed it at the center.

When the devil tempted him in the wilderness, Jesus answered three times from Deuteronomy 6 and 8: man does not live by bread alone (8:3), do not put the Lord your God to the test (6:16), and worship the Lord your God and serve him only (6:13). Israel, whom God had called his son (Exodus 4:22), was tested for forty years in the wilderness and failed at Massah; Jesus, the Son, is tested forty days and keeps faith (Matthew 4:1-11; Luke 4:1-13). Matthew's Gospel develops this pattern of Jesus reliving Israel's story, and the link here is a deliberate typology the evangelists themselves draw, not a later allegory.

Paul reworks the Shema's own words when he writes that for us there is “one God, the Father” and “one Lord, Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 8:6). Richard Bauckham (God Crucified, 1998), N. T. Wright (The Climax of the Covenant, 1991), and Larry Hurtado (One God, One Lord, 1988) have argued, in different ways, that Paul here includes Jesus within the identity of the one God Israel confessed rather than adding a second god beside him. That is how the church came to confess the Trinity without abandoning the Shema. Paul also appeals to the oneness of God to argue that he justifies Jews and Gentiles alike by faith (Romans 3:29-30), and James warns that believing God is one, without the love and obedience the Shema demands, is something even demons manage (James 2:19).

Finally, Deuteronomy itself admits that Israel's heart will need changing: God will circumcise their hearts so that they love him with all their heart and soul (30:6). Jeremiah promises a covenant with the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33), and Paul says that God's love has been poured into believers' hearts through the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:5). Christians read the command of verse 5 as fully kept only by Jesus, and as made possible for others by his Spirit.
interpretation:
Jewish tradition made verses 4 to 9 the center of daily prayer. The Mishnah opens with rules for reciting the Shema evening and morning (m. Berakhot 1:1-4), taking ‘when you lie down and when you get up’ as the times, and it calls the first paragraph taking on the yoke of the kingdom of heaven (m. Berakhot 2:2). In the temple the priests recited it with the Ten Commandments (m. Tamid 5:1). The Talmud tells that Rabbi Akiva, tortured to death by the Romans after the Bar Kokhba revolt (AD 132 to 135), died reciting the Shema and prolonging the word one (b. Berakhot 61b); that Judah the Prince covered his eyes when he recited it (b. Berakhot 13b), the origin of a practice still kept; and that Jacob on his deathbed answered his sons' Shema with the words blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever, which is why that line is said quietly after the first verse (b. Pesachim 56a). The midrash Sifre on Deuteronomy (section 32) takes up verse 5 to distinguish serving God from love and serving him from fear, and to prize the first. Rashi read verse 4 with Zechariah 14:9: the LORD who is now our God alone will one day be one LORD for all nations. Maimonides counted belief in God's unity and love of God among the Torah's positive commandments (Book of the Commandments, positive commandments 2 and 3). Jeffrey Tigay's JPS Torah Commentary (1996) summarizes how Jewish readers have heard the word one against polytheism, dualism, Christian Trinitarianism, and atheism. The Shema is the first prayer many Jewish children learn and the traditional last words of the dying, and Arnold Schoenberg's A Survivor from Warsaw (1947) ends with a men's chorus singing it. The synagogue reads the chapter in the portion Va'etchanan (Deuteronomy 3:23 to 7:11), on the Sabbath of comfort after the fast of the Ninth of Av.

Christian readers received the chapter through Jesus' summary of the law. Augustine (On Christian Teaching, book 1) made love of God and neighbor the goal of all Scripture and a rule for interpreting it: a reading that does not build up that double love has not understood the text. Luther's Small Catechism (1529) explains each of the Ten Commandments with the words that we should fear and love God, the pairing of this chapter. Calvin preached two hundred sermons on Deuteronomy between March 1555 and July 1556 (published 1567, English translation by Arthur Golding, 1583), pressing the Shema on the households and magistrates of Geneva. Protestant family catechesis drew on verse 7 as the charter for teaching faith at home.

Modern study has asked what kind of love and what kind of oneness the text means. Gerhard von Rad (1938), William Moran (1963), and Moshe Weinfeld (Deuteronomy 1-11, Anchor Bible, 1991) set the chapter against ancient treaties. Nathan MacDonald (Deuteronomy and the Meaning of ‘Monotheism’, 2003) argued that the Shema is less an abstract claim about the number of gods than a call to exclusive devotion. Philosophers took up the command itself: Immanuel Kant (Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785) held that love as a feeling cannot be commanded and read the biblical command as practical love, and Søren Kierkegaard (Works of Love, 1847) argued that the ‘you shall’ is what makes love secure against change. In the Revised Common Lectionary verses 1 to 9 are read with Mark 12:28-34 in Year B, in late autumn.
text:
English Bibles differ most visibly in verse 4, because the Hebrew has six words and no verb: YHWH eloheinu YHWH echad. The words can be grouped as ‘The LORD our God, the LORD is one’ (BSB, ESV), ‘The LORD our God is one LORD’ (KJV), ‘The LORD is our God, the LORD is one’, or ‘The LORD is our God, the LORD alone’ (NJPS, NRSV). The first three stress God's unity or uniqueness; the last stresses Israel's exclusive loyalty. All are grammatically possible, and the readings overlap. In Hebrew scrolls and printed Bibles the last letters of shema and echad are written large; together they spell ed, witness.

The Septuagint and the Nash Papyrus place a heading before verse 4 that the Masoretic Text lacks, describing these as the statutes and judgments commanded in the wilderness after the exodus. The Septuagint renders verse 4 ‘the Lord our God is one Lord’, the wording of Mark 12:29. In verse 5, Septuagint manuscripts differ over the first term, some reading heart and others mind, and the Gospels quote the command with three terms (Matthew 22:37) or four (Mark 12:30), probably because the Hebrew levav covers both heart and mind. Other differences are translation choices: ‘teach them diligently’ (KJV, BSB) or ‘recite them’ (NRSV) in verse 7; ‘frontlets between thine eyes’ (KJV) or ‘bind them on your foreheads’ in verse 8; ‘strength’ or ‘might’ in verse 5. The tefillin and mezuzot from Qumran preserve these verses with small variations in spelling and wording. Hebrew and English verse numbers are the same in this chapter.

teach.big: Because the LORD alone is Israel's God and has rescued them, he is to be loved with the whole self, and that love is kept alive by his words in every room of life and by remembering him most carefully in times of plenty.

outline.t: God's commands are given to be taught and lived across generations, and their aim is reverent loyalty that leads to life.
Who God is comes before what God asks: the one LORD claims the whole person, heart, life, and every resource.
Love for God is sustained by keeping his words inside first, then in the home, on the road, in the body, and in public life.
Prosperity is dangerous because it hides the Giver behind the gifts; remembering is an act of loyalty, and forgetting leads to other gods.
Trust does not demand that God prove himself on our terms; it does what is right and good in his sight and leaves the promises to him.
When children ask why we obey, the answer is a story of rescue: grace comes first, and the commands are given for our good.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first treats verse 4 as a weapon in the argument over the Trinity, as though the verse either disproves it or secretly teaches it through the word echad. The verse's own weight falls on the LORD alone being Israel's God, and Christians confess the Trinity as an account of that one God, not as a proof drawn from a numeral. The second reduces the command to love to a feeling that must be manufactured, which leaves sincere people anxious; in Deuteronomy love is allegiance shown in listening and obeying, and God promises to give the heart that loves him (30:6). The third turns verses 6 to 9 into a technique for religious parenting, as if the right routine guarantees faithful children. The text commands faithful teaching, but the chapter's own warnings show that each generation must choose.

Teachers should also avoid two opposite errors with verses 10 to 12. One reads them as a condemnation of wealth as such; the land's goodness is God's gift, and the problem is forgetting, not eating. The other skips them altogether, though they are the chapter's longest warning. Finally, verse 25 should not be taught as a formula for earning salvation, nor dismissed as Old Testament legalism. The parent's answer begins with ‘we were slaves’ and God's rescue, and obedience comes as the life of the rescued.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on parents, especially those whose grown children have left the faith, who may hear verses 7 to 9 as a verdict on their failure. The text lays responsibility on parents to teach, but it does not promise that teaching controls the outcome, and it addresses every generation as needing to hear for itself. It may also press on people raised in homes where Scripture was used to control or shame them, for whom constant religious talk was not love. Teach the chapter's picture of faith as a story of rescue told to a child's honest question, not as pressure. Some in the room will feel they cannot love God with all their heart and will doubt they belong at all; they need to hear that Deuteronomy itself promises that God will circumcise the heart, and that the command to love is answered first by God's love for them.

hard.q: If the Shema says the LORD is one, how can Christians confess the Trinity?
hard.a:
The objection is ancient and serious. Jewish interpreters have heard the Shema as ruling out any plurality in God. Maimonides made the unity of God, a oneness unlike any other, one of his Thirteen Principles and codified it as the foundation of the law (Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:7), and medieval Jewish disputants pressed the verse against Christian doctrine; Jeffrey Tigay's commentary notes that Jewish readers have long heard in echad a denial of the Trinity. Islam makes a similar claim about the oneness of God, and within Christian history the Socinians of the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and later Unitarians argued that the Trinity is a departure from the Shema. On this view, confessing Jesus as divine necessarily adds a second God.

Christians have answered in several ways. The first is historical: the earliest Christians were Jews who kept reciting the Shema. Larry Hurtado (One God, One Lord, 1988) argued that devotion to Jesus arose early among Jewish believers who did not think they had abandoned monotheism, and Richard Bauckham (God Crucified, 1998) and N. T. Wright (The Climax of the Covenant, 1991) read 1 Corinthians 8:6 as placing Jesus within the identity of the one God named in the Shema. The second is theological: the creeds of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) confess one God, and the doctrine of the Trinity was framed precisely to keep the Shema while confessing what the church believed about the Son and the Spirit. The persons are not three gods but the one God, Father, Son, and Spirit. The third is exegetical: some Christian writers have pointed to the plural form elohim or to echad as hints of plurality, though many Christian scholars regard those arguments as weak and prefer to rest the doctrine on the New Testament's witness. The church confesses the Trinity as first-order faith; the disagreement with Jewish and Muslim readers is real and should be stated honestly, without pretending the Shema itself settles it for either side.

hard.q: Verse 25 says keeping the commands will be Israel's righteousness. Does that mean salvation is earned by obedience?
hard.a:
Read on its own, verse 25 can sound like a formula for earning God's favor, and some readers have heard it that way. Critics of the Old Testament from Marcion in the second century onward set law against grace, and some Protestant readers have taken verses like this as the law's offer of life on condition of perfect obedience, citing Paul's use of Leviticus 18:5, “The man who does these things will live by them” (Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12), and his statement that no one will be justified by works of the law (Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16). On that reading the verse sets a standard sinful people cannot meet.

Other readers stress the verse's setting. The parent's answer begins with rescue, not effort: “We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out” (verse 21). Righteousness in Deuteronomy names faithful conduct within a covenant God has already made, as in 24:13, where returning a pledged cloak is ‘righteousness for you before the LORD’. Jewish interpreters have long read the Torah as a gracious gift to a people already chosen. E. P. Sanders (Paul and Palestinian Judaism, 1977) called this pattern covenantal nomism: one enters the covenant by God's grace and stays in it by obedience, with provision for atonement. Advocates of the new perspective on Paul, including James Dunn and N. T. Wright, read Paul's critique of works of the law as aimed chiefly at the law's role in marking Israel off from the nations. Lutheran and Reformed interpreters, among them Stephen Westerholm (Perspectives Old and New on Paul, 2004), have replied that Paul still sets human doing against God's gift. Christians read the relation between Deuteronomy and Paul differently, and the question is second-order; all these readings agree that in Deuteronomy grace comes before obedience, not after it, and that Paul himself quotes Deuteronomy 30:12-14 to describe the righteousness of faith (Romans 10:6-8).

observe: What three things are Israel to love God with in verse 5, and where in the day and in the household are God's words to be kept in verses 7 to 9?
List the things in verses 10 and 11 that Israel did not build, fill, dig, or plant. What does Moses say will happen when they eat and are satisfied?
When the child asks what the commandments mean in verse 20, how does the parent's answer begin, and what does it say the commands were given for?
interpret: Why do you think the confession of verse 4 comes before the command of verse 5? What difference does the order make?
Why would plenty make people forget God more easily than hunger did? What does it mean in Hebrew to forget someone?
How does the parent's answer in verses 21 to 25 shape the meaning of the word righteousness in verse 25?
apply: Which part of your life (your thinking, your very life, or your resources) do you find hardest to include in loving God?
Where has comfort, rather than hardship, made you less aware of your need for God, and what practice of remembering could answer it?
If a child or a friend asked you why you live the way you do as a believer, what story would you tell?
